unit.name: Generated code and technical debt
unit.description: Laurence explains why vibe coding does not remove the need for engineering skill and uses technical debt to evaluate generated-code tradeoffs.
unit.summary: Laurence rejects the simplistic meme that generated code makes engineers less useful; instead, skilled engineers become better at using and judging generated code [ts=2861s]. He introduces technical debt as the main framework for reasoning about AI-generated code, comparing good debt to a mortgage and bad debt to high-interest impulse spending [ts=2947s]. Every software artifact creates future obligations such as bugs, support, documentation, new features, marketing, and feedback loops [ts=3015s]. He warns that repeated prompting can create spaghetti code and that organizational authority can push low-quality generated code into shared codebases [ts=3282s].

key_points.text: The more skilled an engineer is, the better they become at using generated-code workflows.
Technical debt is introduced as a framework for understanding vibe coding and generated code.
Every build creates future obligations such as bugs, support, documentation, features, and feedback.
Repeated prompting can spiral into spaghetti code, especially when generated APIs target the wrong platform.
A bad organizational pattern is authority-over-merit generated code that engineers later have to fix.
